newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban reports push towards key valley.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban reports push towards key valley.

text.p: Afghanistan's Taleban Islamic militia said it had pushed towards the key opposition-held Panjsher valley on Sunday from the strategic Gulbahar district, and asked civilians to leave Gulbahar.

The militia captured three villages and large quantities of weapons from the forces of the ousted government in an offensive that began in the morning, Taleban's Voice of Sharia radio said. Many opposition fighters were killed.
Earlier, a Taleban commander and civilians said the militia was continuing to expel civilians from Gulbahar district to prevent any uprising by them.

"We have told people to leave the area because they pass on military information to our opposition and to prevent any kind of revolt against our Taleban brothers," the militia's frontline commander Mir Ahmad said.

The largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban seized the opposition strongholds of Jabal-os-Siraj and Gulbahar on Thursday in the latest northward drive against a coalition of mainly Tajik forces loyal to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani and of northern Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Earlier, the Islamic militia had told civilians nearby in newly-captured Charikar, capital of Parwan province, and areas around the Bagram airbase to vacate their homes, sending thousands of people fleeing to Kabul.
Gulbahar, 90 km (55 miles) north of the Taleban-ruled capital, is a small town at the mouth of the Panjsher valley, the stronghold of ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood.
The Taleban forces control the mountain to the left of Gulbahar road overlooking Panjsher, from where their artillery fired on Masood's forces inside the valley on Sunday.

Gulbahar appeared totally deserted except for elderly people and women waiting for buses and trucks to take them out. Angry locals gathered at a bus stop said they did not want to leave their homes but the Taleban would not let them stay.

"We sent a delegation of our area to see the Taleban to say that there will be no insurgency from our side against them," one villager said. "We stated that we are your subjects. The Taleban did not agree and told us to leave."
Another villager said: "We swore on the holy Koran that we will not cause any uprising, but it fell on deaf ears."
The bodies of two opposition fighters killed last week still lay on the side of the main road north of Kabul as an apparent warning to locals against causing any trouble for the militia.
"We are ready to die under rocket and mortar shells in our village, but do not want to leave it because we have nowhere to go and settle down," an elderly man said.
He said the only place the local residents could go was Kabul, where there was not much hope for them either.
Local residents say they lack currency valid in Kabul and relatives to stay with in the capital.

A survey carried out by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says some 50,000 people have recently been displaced from north of Kabul. Most are living in schools and other government buldings, with few belongings and little cash.
An estimated 11,100 families are still in various districts north of Kabul and have not been able to come to the capital for lack of cash to hire transport.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) says it will distribute relief to people who unable to get to Kabul.
A U.N. official told reporters that Taleban authorities had promised help in relief distribution and a return to normality in the area north of Kabul.
